passages.v01:c01:p0001: A great many individuals, both inside Brierley and beyond, are able to pay strict attention to the affairs of their neighbors by virtue of ignoring their own; Mrs. Agatha Sowerby, however, belonged to that category of proficient women who are able to handle their personal affairs while simultaneously directing those of everyone else. Being an outstanding homemaker, her chores were perpetually finished and thoroughly executed; she directed the Sewing Circle, assisted in directing the Sunday-school, and served as the primary pillar of both the Church Aid Society and the Foreign Missions Auxiliary. Despite all these responsibilities, Mrs. Agatha discovered plenty of leisure to remain seated for hours beside her kitchen window, producing “cotton warp” quilts with her knitting needles—she had completed sixteen such items, a detail Brierley homemakers were accustomed to sharing in hushed, respectful tones—and maintaining a vigilant watch over the principal thoroughfare that traversed the valley and climbed the sharp red incline past it. Because Brierley was situated upon a tiny triangular strip of land projecting into the Gulf of St. Lawrence, surrounded by water on two sides, anyone entering or leaving the community was required to travel along that hillside path and thereby navigate the invisible scrutiny of Mrs. Agatha’s perceptive gaze.
